result.area: Cloudflare Workers, Queues, and Hyperdrive — current limits and pricing (accessed 2026-08-16)
result.summary: All values below were fetched from developers.cloudflare.com and cloudflare.com on 2026-08-16; none are from memory. Workers Paid is $5 USD/month minimum, including 10 million requests and 30 million CPU-milliseconds; overage is $0.30 per additional million requests and $0.02 per additional million CPU-ms, with no charge for duration (wall clock), egress, or bandwidth. The Free plan's binding constraints are 10 ms CPU per invocation and 100,000 requests/day; Paid raises CPU to a default 30 seconds configurable to a 5-minute ceiling. Cloudflare's docs state "There is no general limit on requests per second" for Workers and publish no per-account concurrency cap — the practical ceilings are 128 MB memory per isolate, 6 simultaneous open outbound connections per invocation, 10,000 subrequests per invocation (configurable up to 10M), and 100 Workers on Free / 500 on Paid per account. The documented failure mode for CPU exhaustion is explicit and client-visible: Cloudflare returns Error 1102 with "Worker exceeded resource limits", surfacing in the dashboard as "Exceeded CPU Time Limits" — a hard error page, not graceful degradation, which matters for Liquid/React theme rendering in the storefront. Cloudflare Queues costs $0.40 per million operations with 1,000,000 operations/month included on Workers Paid (10,000 operations/day on Free); an operation is each 64 KB written, read, or deleted, so a typical write-read-delete lifecycle is 3 operations per small message and every retry adds a read. The hard Queues ceilings that matter are 5,000 messages/second per queue, 25 GB backlog per queue, 250 concurrent consumer invocations, 100 messages per batch, 60-second batch wait, 128 KB message size, 100 retries, and 10,000 queues per account. Queues delivery is explicitly at-least-once ("may be delivered more than once") and explicitly unordered ("Queues does not guarantee that messages will be delivered to a consumer in the same order in which they are published") — both are load-bearing for a payment/ledger platform and are already covered by LetBuyy's idempotency_key discipline. Without a configured Dead Letter Queue, messages that exhaust retries "are deleted permanently"; a DLQ with no active consumer holds messages 4 days. Hyperdrive is included at no extra cost on Workers Paid (unlimited queries; Free is capped at 100,000 queries/day and ~20 origin connections) and is the most important capacity lever here: it runs a transaction-mode pooler placed "in one or more regions closest to your origin database" and "automatically manages the connection pool properties for you, including limiting the total number of connections to your origin database" — approximately 100 origin connections per Hyperdrive configuration on Paid, independent of how many Worker isolates are running. Hyperdrive's query cache defaults to max_age 60 s and stale_while_revalidate 15 s (max_age up to 3,600 s) and critically "does not purge or invalidate cached read query results when your application writes to your database", so any read that must reflect a write (cart, inventory, order status, auth) needs a second `--caching-disabled` binding. Hyperdrive supports PostgreSQL 9.0–17.x, and Cloudflare's own Supabase guide says to use the Direct connection string rather than Supabase's pooled (Supavisor) strings and a real Postgres driver rather than the supabase-js client; SQL-level PREPARE/DEALLOCATE/EXECUTE, advisory locks, and LISTEN/NOTIFY are unsupported through Hyperdrive. For India, Cloudflare's network page lists roughly two dozen Indian cities across 348 cities globally, and India IS an available region for Regional Services (Enterprise-only paid add-on, price unpublished), but Customer Metadata Boundary can only be set to the United States or the European Union — there is no India metadata boundary at any price. Rate limiting is severely plan-gated: 1 rule / IP-only / 10 s period on Free, 2 rules on Pro, 5 rules with custom counting expressions on Business, 100 rules with header/cookie/JSON-field/path counting only on Enterprise Advanced Rate Limiting — per-tenant (site_id) rate limiting effectively requires Enterprise. The published uptime SLA is 100% on Business ($200/mo billed annually, $250 monthly, per domain) and Enterprise only; Free and Pro carry no SLA, and the remedy is service credits, not a technical guarantee. Cloudflare Inc. has been registered for Indian GST since 1 October 2023, so Indian GST applies on top of every USD figure here and the GSTIN must be on the billing profile before the cycle (it cannot be applied retroactively).

result.capacity_implications:
WHAT BREAKS FIRST, IN ORDER.

1) POSTGRES CONNECTIONS ARE NOT THE FIRST WALL — IF AND ONLY IF LETBUYY ACTUALLY USES HYPERDRIVE. Cloudflare's own statement is that Hyperdrive "automatically manages the connection pool properties for you, including limiting the total number of connections to your origin database", quantified as ~100 origin connections per Hyperdrive configuration on Workers Paid (~20 on Free). So N concurrent Worker isolates do NOT consume N Postgres connections; they multiplex over ~100 connections in transaction mode. Arithmetic: with a mean DB-side transaction time of 40 ms, 100 connections yield 100 / 0.040 = 2,500 transactions/second. At 200 ms per transaction (a fat create_checkout_order doing FOR UPDATE plus ledger inserts plus GST computation) that collapses to 100 / 0.200 = 500 tx/s. At 500 ms it is 200/s. The scaling lever is therefore RPC latency, not Worker count: halving RPC duration doubles platform throughput. Secondary levers: split read and write traffic across separate Hyperdrive configs (25 max on Paid, so up to ~2,500 pooled connections in aggregate — at which point Supabase's own max_connections becomes the binding cap), and shard tenants across Supabase projects. CRITICAL CAVEAT FOR THIS REPO: Cloudflare explicitly tells Supabase users to use the DIRECT connection string with a node-postgres or postgres.js driver and NOT the supabase-js client. LetBuyy's canonical money path is db.rpc through supabase-js / getSupabaseAdmin (115 files), which is PostgREST over HTTPS — that traffic does not traverse Hyperdrive at all and receives none of this pooling. In that architecture the connection ceiling is Supabase's own pooler (Supavisor) plus PostgREST's internal pool, and every Hyperdrive number above is inapplicable. Resolving which path is actually in use is the highest-value prerequisite before any connection arithmetic in the capacity model is trusted.

2) HYPERDRIVE'S CACHE IS A CORRECTNESS HAZARD BEFORE IT IS A CAPACITY WIN. Default max_age 60 s plus stale_while_revalidate 15 s, and "Hyperdrive does not purge or invalidate cached read query results when your application writes to your database." For commerce that means inventory counts, cart contents, order status, gift-card balances and session/permission reads can be served up to 75 seconds stale after a write. The mitigation is structural, not tunable: a second Hyperdrive binding created with --caching-disabled for all read-after-write and auth paths, consuming 2 of the 25 config slots per database. Note also that anything using NOW() or CURRENT_DATE is never cached anyway, so time-bounded queries get no benefit.

3) WORKERS CPU IS THE FIRST COST WALL AND THE FIRST STOREFRONT FAILURE MODE. Requests are nearly free: 100M requests/month costs (100 − 10) × $0.30 = $27 on top of the $5 base. CPU dominates: at 15 ms mean CPU, 100M requests = 1,500M CPU-ms, of which 1,470M is billable → 1,470 × $0.02 = $29.40. Total ≈ $61/month. At 60 ms mean CPU (heavy Liquid render plus sanitiser), the same 100M requests = 6,000M CPU-ms → 5,970 × $0.02 = $119.40; at 200 ms → $399. Cost is roughly linear in CPU per render. The failure mode is worse than the cost: exceeding the CPU limit returns Cloudflare Error 1102 "Worker exceeded resource limits" straight to the shopper — a Cloudflare error page mid-checkout, not a degraded render. The Paid default is 30 s (5 min ceiling) so this only bites on pathological theme loops, but it means an untrusted merchant theme can produce a hard 1102 rather than a timeout-and-fallback. Set limits.cpu_ms explicitly per Worker to bound both blast radius and bill.

4) THE 6 SIMULTANEOUS OPEN CONNECTIONS PER INVOCATION LIMIT IS THE QUIET ONE. Identical on Free and Paid, not raisable. Any storefront render that fans out in parallel to gateway plus theme plus product plus inventory plus reviews plus recommendations plus analytics will serialise past 6, silently converting parallel latency into additive latency. Design fan-out width to <= 6 or batch server-side. By contrast the 10,000 subrequests per invocation limit (raisable to 10M) is not a practical constraint.

5) QUEUES HITS A HARD WALL AT 5,000 MESSAGES/SECOND PER QUEUE AND 250 CONCURRENT CONSUMERS. 5,000 msg/s equals ~432 million messages/day per queue — well beyond near-term need, but the consumer side binds much earlier. Drain rate = max_concurrency × batch_size / batch_duration. At the 250/100 ceiling: a 100-message batch finishing in 5 s gives 250 × 100 / 5 = 5,000 msg/s, exactly matching the ingest cap. If each message costs a 100 ms Postgres RPC processed serially, a 100-message batch takes 10 s and drain falls to 2,500 msg/s — backlog then grows at any higher ingest rate, and the 25 GB per-queue backlog cap (~25M messages at 1 KB each) becomes the countdown to "Storage Limit Exceeded". Compounding interaction with (1): 250 concurrent consumers each holding a Postgres transaction would want 250 connections but only ~100 exist per Hyperdrive config, so the queue tier and the request tier contend for the same pool and starve each other under load. Levers: shard workloads across queues (10,000 per account), parallelise inside the consumer (bounded by the 6 open connections), and shorten the RPC.

6) QUEUES SEMANTICS ALIGN WITH THE LEDGER RULES, WITH ONE GAP. At-least-once delivery and explicitly no ordering guarantee are both already satisfied by LetBuyy's mandatory idempotency_key plus ON CONFLICT discipline. The gap is DLQ configuration: "Without a DLQ configured, messages that reach the retry limit are deleted permanently." A payment-confirmation or webhook-fanout job vanishing silently after 3 retries is unacceptable on a money path — every money-adjacent queue needs an explicit DLQ, and the DLQ itself needs a consumer, because DLQ messages without an active consumer are deleted after 4 days. Also, batches are all-or-nothing on retry by default, so one poison message re-delivers up to 99 already-processed siblings; idempotency must hold at message granularity, and explicit per-message ack should be used on money jobs.

7) QUEUES COST IS TRIVIAL AT LETBUYY SCALE. Cloudflare's own example: 1M messages/day for 30 days = 90M operations = $35.60/month after the 1M free allowance. At 1,000 merchants × 100 orders/day = 100k orders/day with ~10 async jobs per order = 1M messages/day, that is the same ~$36/month. Keep messages under 64 KB (128 KB is the hard max) or every action costs 2 operations instead of 1 — put payloads in R2 or the DB and enqueue identifiers only.

8) INDIA AND REGULATORY POSTURE IS THE EXPENSIVE CONSTRAINT. Cloudflare has extensive Indian PoPs (Mumbai, New Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and more within 348 global cities) and India IS an available Regional Services region — but Regional Services is Enterprise-only, publicly unpriced, and incompatible with HTTP/3. Customer Metadata Boundary can only be set to the United States or the European Union, so Cloudflare cannot keep LetBuyy's logs and analytics metadata inside India at any price today. If a DPDP/RBI-driven localisation requirement lands, that is a hard product gap, not a config change. Separately there is no user-selectable ap-south Workers region: placement is nearest-eyeball by default or Smart Placement near the origin. Since the Postgres origin is the latency-dominant hop (Cloudflare's own figures: 20–30 ms cross-region vs 1–3 ms local per query), Smart Placement plus a Mumbai-region Supabase is the correct configuration, and every extra sequential query multiplies that 20–30 ms delta.

9) SECURITY TIERING FORCES A PLAN UPGRADE EARLIER THAN COST DOES. Per-tenant rate limiting (per site_id, per store subdomain, per customer cookie) requires counting by Header / Cookie / JSON field / Path — Enterprise Advanced Rate Limiting only. Business gives 5 rules and custom counting expressions but only IP and IP-with-NAT counting characteristics, which cannot express per-merchant fairness; Free gives 1 rule, IP only, 10 s period, 10 s block. For a platform whose login, OTP and checkout endpoints are the abuse surface, Business ($200/mo/domain billed annually) is the realistic floor and Enterprise is where per-tenant controls become expressible at all. Sensitive Data Detection (PII/financial download monitoring) is likewise Enterprise-only. The 100% uptime SLA also starts only at Business and is a service-credit remedy, not an availability guarantee.

10) TAX. Cloudflare Inc. has been GST-registered in India since 1 October 2023, so every USD figure above is pre-GST and Indian GST will be added to invoices. The GSTIN must be on the billing profile before the cycle because it cannot be applied retroactively to issued invoices. The exact GST rate Cloudflare applies is not stated on its tax page.

I independently fetched https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/ (and its raw markdown twin, .../limits/index.md), https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/, and the changelog https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2025-03-25-higher-cpu-limits/ on 2026-08-16. Every one of the 12 claimed values matches the vendor's current published text. Nothing required correction.

Verified verbatim, per fact:
1. Requests/day — Account plan limits table: Workers Free "100,000/day", Workers Paid "No limit". CONFIRMED. Free cap is HARD-with-choice: the "Daily requests" section says the limit resets at midnight UTC and exceeding it returns Error 1027, with a per-route "Fail open" (bypass the Worker) vs "Fail closed" (serve the 1027 page) mode.
2. Requests per second / burst — the exact sentence "Workers scale automatically across the Cloudflare global network. There is no general limit on requests per second." is present, sitting under the "Daily requests" heading. CONFIRMED. Important caveat for the capacity model, and the one thing I stress-tested hardest: a WebSearch result asserted a Workers Free "burst rate limit of 1,000 requests per minute" with error 1015 / HTTP 429. I checked for this three ways — a full heading dump of the page (no "Burst rate" heading exists; headings run Account plan limits, Request and response limits, CPU time, Memory, Duration, Daily requests, Subrequests, Worker-to-Worker subrequests, Simultaneous open connections, Environment variables, Worker size, Worker startup time, Number of Workers, Routes and domains, Routes with wrangler dev --remote, Cache API limits, Log size, Image Resizing, Static Assets, Unbound and Bundled plan limits, Wall time limits by invocation type, Related resources), a literal string search for "burst" / "1,000 requests per minute" / "1015" (all absent), and the workers.dev routing page (no rate-limit statement). That burst figure is a stale/removed limit surfacing from a search index, NOT current vendor text. The researcher's claim matches the live page and is correct. For planning purposes: Cloudflare publishes no RPS or burst ceiling, so RPS headroom is UNKNOWN-by-design rather than guaranteed-unlimited, and anti-abuse rate limiting has historically existed on Free — do not model Free as burst-unlimited.
3. CPU time per HTTP request — CPU time table: Free "10 ms", Paid "5 min (default: 30 seconds)". The "Increasing the CPU time limit" subsection confirms Workers Paid, key `limits.cpu_ms`, max 300000 with the comment "default is 30000 (30 seconds)", plus a dashboard path (Workers & Pages > Worker > Settings). The 2025-03-25 changelog independently corroborates 5 min / 300,000 ms max and 30 s default. CONFIRMED. Free 10 ms = HARD; Paid = DEFAULT/configurable to a HARD 300,000 ms ceiling.
4. CPU time per Cron Trigger — Free "10 ms"; Paid "30 seconds (< 1 hour interval)", "15 min (>= 1 hour interval)". CONFIRMED.
5. Failure mode — "When a Worker exceeds its CPU time limit, Cloudflare returns Error 1102 to the client with the message `Worker exceeded resource limits`", shown as "Exceeded CPU Time Limits" under Metrics > Errors > Invocation Statuses. CONFIRMED, and I'd add the analytics/Logpush outcome string `exceededCpu` for instrumentation. Note 1102 is shared with the memory limit (that path surfaces as "Exceeded Memory"), so 1102 alone does not disambiguate CPU vs memory exhaustion.
6. Duration — "Duration measures wall-clock time from start to end of a Worker invocation"; table: HTTP request "No limit", Cron Trigger / Durable Object Alarm / Queue Consumer "15 min"; prose confirms "As long as the client remains connected, the Worker can continue processing, making subrequests, and streaming a response body." The separate "Wall time limits by invocation type" table agrees and adds Durable Objects (RPC/HTTP) "Unlimited" and Workflows (per step) "Unlimited". Not-billed is confirmed on the pricing page: "No charge or limit for duration" (Standard/Paid) and "No charge for duration" (Free). CONFIRMED.
7. Memory per isolate — "Each isolate can consume up to 128 MB of memory, including the JavaScript heap and WebAssembly allocations"; table 128 MB for both Free and Paid. CONFIRMED. Modelling note: this is per isolate, not per request, and one isolate may serve concurrent requests.
8. Startup time — table "Startup time: 1 second"; prose "A Worker must parse and execute its global scope (top-level code outside of handlers) within 1 second". CONFIRMED numerically. One wording nuance worth carrying into the model: the current docs label this "Worker startup time" / "Startup time", not "startup CPU time" as the fact was phrased. The value 1 second is correct for both plans; the older 400 ms figure some sources still quote is not on the current page.
9. Subrequests per invocation — Free "50", Paid "10,000 (up to 10M)", with "You can change the subrequest limit per Worker using the limits configuration in your Wrangler configuration file", and "Each subrequest in a redirect chain counts against this limit". CONFIRMED, including the "up to 10M" adjustability. Free 50 = HARD; Paid = DEFAULT/configurable.
10. Internal-service subrequests — Free "1,000", Paid "Matches configured limit (default 10,000)". CONFIRMED. Directly relevant to LetBuyy: KV, R2, D1 and service-binding calls consume this budget.
11. Simultaneous open outbound connections — "Each Worker invocation can have up to six connections simultaneously waiting for response headers", 6 on both plans. CONFIRMED, HARD, identical Free/Paid. This is the real fan-out ceiling for parallel Supabase/gateway calls per invocation.

Region/pricing note (not among the facts, but load-bearing context I checked while verifying): the Workers pricing page publishes USD only — Paid $5/month per account, 10 million requests included then +$0.30 per additional million, 30 million CPU-milliseconds included then +$0.02 per additional million CPU-ms. It contains no India/ap-south regional pricing and no GST statement; GST applicability is UNKNOWN from this page and would need Cloudflare's billing/tax documentation or an invoice to settle. None of the compute limits above are region-specific — they are global and identical for ap-south execution.

result.area: Cloudflare KV, R2, D1, and Durable Objects — limits, consistency, and pricing (accessed 2026-08-16)
result.summary: All values below were fetched from developers.cloudflare.com on 2026-08-16; nothing is from memory. The two numbers that decide architecture for LetBuyy are both in Workers KV: (1) writes to the SAME key are capped at 1 per second on Free and Paid alike, and exceeding it throws HTTP 429 — Cloudflare's own words are "Workers KV has a maximum of 1 write to the same key per second. Writes made to the same key within 1 second will cause rate limiting (429) errors to be thrown"; and (2) the eventual-consistency window is "may take up to 60 seconds or more to be visible in other global network locations", with a per-read cacheTtl whose default is 60 s and minimum is 30 s. Cloudflare explicitly states KV "is not ideal for applications where you need support for atomic operations or where values must be read and written in a single transaction", nor for write-heavy workloads updating the same key "tens or hundreds of times per second". That rules KV out as a rate-limit backend, a counter, a session store, or a cache-version key that any single tenant might bump more than once per second — and it makes KV unsafe for anything price-, inventory-, or entitlement-critical inside a 60-second window. KV remains excellent and very cheap for read-heavy tenant config: 10 M reads/month included then $0.50/million, 1 GB storage then $0.50/GB-month; writes/deletes/lists are 10× the read price at $5.00/million each. R2 is the strongest fit in the stack for an India-first image-heavy catalogue: $0.015/GB-month Standard, Class A $4.50/million, Class B $0.36/million, and egress is explicitly free "via the Workers API, S3 API, and r2.dev domains"; max object 5 TiB (4.995 TiB multipart), 5 GiB single-part, 10,000 parts, 1,000,000 buckets/account, 1,000 lifecycle rules/bucket. R2's only per-object throttle is "Concurrent writes to the same object name (key) at a higher rate return HTTP 429" at 1/second; there is no documented per-prefix request-rate limit (unlike S3), and bucket *management* ops are capped at 50/second, with the REST API capped at 1,200 requests per five minutes account-wide. D1 is SQLite with a hard 10 GB per-database ceiling (500 MB Free), 50,000 databases/account, 1 TB storage/account, 1,000 queries per Worker invocation, 30 s max query duration, and 6 simultaneous connections per invocation; Cloudflare publishes NO write-throughput number, and the architecture is a single primary that all writes must reach, with read replication still described in release notes as public beta (2025-04-10) requiring the Sessions API for sequential consistency. Cloudflare positions D1 as "designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases" — i.e. sharded, read-heavy, not a shared multi-tenant ledger. D1 pricing is asymmetric by 1000×: rows read are $0.001/million after 25 billion/month included, rows written are $1.00/million after 50 million/month, storage $0.75/GB-month after 5 GB. Durable Objects are the correct coordination primitive but have a documented "soft limit of 1,000 requests per second" per individual object because "each individual Object is inherently single-threaded"; the Rules page gives ~500–1,000 rps for simple operations and warns that "a single Durable Object handling all traffic becomes a bottleneck... A common mistake is using a Durable Object for global rate limiting or global counters." An overloaded object "will, after attempting to queue them, return an overloaded error to the caller", and the prescribed remedy is sharding: Required DOs = (total rps) / (per-DO capacity). SQLite-backed DOs are now the recommended and effectively only backend for new namespaces (10 GB storage per object, 2 MB combined key+value, 100 columns/table, 100 KB SQL statement); DO pricing is $0.15/million requests (WebSocket messages billed 20:1) plus $12.50/million GB-s of duration measured at 128 MB (0.128 GB-s per wall-second), with 1 M requests and 400,000 GB-s included monthly, and WebSocket Hibernation removing duration charges while idle. Two India-specific constraints matter: Durable Object placement offers only apac / apac-ne / apac-se location hints (best-effort, never moved after creation) and jurisdictions limited to EU / US / FedRAMP — there is no India jurisdiction — while Cloudflare "is registered for Goods and Services Tax (GST) purposes in India as of October 1st, 2023" and bills tax by billing address, so all USD prices above are pre-GST for an Indian entity.

facts.subject: Cloudflare Workers KV
facts.metric: Writes to the SAME key (hot-key write rate)
facts.value: 1 per second (exceeding it throws HTTP 429: "Workers KV has a maximum of 1 write to the same key per second. Writes made to the same key within 1 second will cause rate limiting (429) errors to be thrown.")
facts.note: THE critical number. Same value published on the limits table ("Writes to same key: 1 per second") for both plans. Mitigation documented: consolidate writes within an invocation, wait >=1s, or retry with exponential backoff. This is a per-key limit only; writes spread across different keys are not subject to it.

facts.subject: Cloudflare Workers KV
facts.value: "Changes may take up to 60 seconds or more to be visible in other global network locations as their cached versions of the data time out." Writes are "usually immediately visible" only at the location where made.
facts.note: THE second critical number. Note the wording is "60 seconds OR MORE" — Cloudflare does not guarantee an upper bound. Read docs add: "get() and getWithMetadata() methods may return stale values... may take up to 60 seconds (or the duration of the cacheTtl) to display."

facts.subject: Cloudflare Workers KV
facts.value: "The cacheTtl parameter must be an integer greater than or equal to 30. 60 is the default." Maximum value is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.

NOT FOR: "applications where you need support for atomic operations or where values must be read and written in a single transaction", nor write-heavy workloads updating the same key "tens or hundreds of times per second".

result.capacity_implications:
WHAT BREAKS FIRST: the KV single-key write limit, at essentially zero load. It is 1 write/sec/key on both plans and returns HTTP 429, so any design where a per-tenant or per-resource key is bumped by concurrent requests fails immediately, not at scale. Concretely for LetBuyy: (a) KV CANNOT be the rate-limit backend — a per-site_id or per-IP counter key would need N writes/sec by definition and will 429 on the second request in the same second; use a sharded Durable Object or Cloudflare's Rate Limiting binding instead; (b) a cache-version / theme-version key per store breaks the moment a merchant saves twice in one second (bulk product import, theme publish, a double-clicked Save) — this is a 2-request failure, not a 1,000-request one; (c) session or step-up-token state in KV is wrong on both counts (write rate + the 60s window). Mitigation if KV is retained for versioning: write to key+timestamp-bucket, or debounce writes server-side to <=1/sec/key with exponential-backoff retry as Cloudflare's own sample does.

SECOND FAILURE — CORRECTNESS, NOT CAPACITY: the eventual-consistency window is "up to 60 seconds OR MORE" with cacheTtl default 60s (min 30s). A merchant changes a price or a product goes out of stock; another PoP serves the old value for up to a minute. For a checkout that must be server-authoritative on totals, that is a money bug, so prices, inventory, gift-card balances and GST rates must never be read from KV on the money path. KV is safe for tenant routing metadata (host -> site_id), feature flags, and theme config where a 60s lag is tolerable. Note the shared 1,000-operations-per-invocation budget spans KV AND R2 subrequests together.

THIRD — THE DURABLE OBJECT SERIALIZATION CEILING: soft limit 1,000 rps per object (Rules page: ~500-1,000 rps for simple ops, lower with JSON serialization or list()). Arithmetic for the sharding plan: at 100 merchants averaging 5 rps peak each = 500 rps aggregate — trivially fine IF sharded per site_id (each merchant is ~5 rps, 0.5% of one object's budget). At 10,000 merchants x 20 rps peak = 200,000 rps aggregate, still fine per-shard, because the per-object number is what matters, not the total. What is NOT fine is any singleton: one global rate limiter, one platform-wide order counter, one inventory coordinator — that funnels everything into a single thread, queues, then returns an overloaded error. The scaling lever is Cloudflare's own formula, Required DOs = total rps / per-DO capacity, keyed by idFromName(site_id) or idFromName(site_id + ":" + sku). Rule of thumb from the numbers: never let one logical key exceed ~500 rps of real work; shard at site_id first, then site_id+resource. India-specific caveat: there is no India location hint (only apac / apac-ne / apac-se, best-effort) and no India jurisdiction (EU/US/FedRAMP only), and "Durable Objects do not currently change locations after they are created" — so a per-merchant DO created by a request originating outside India is pinned outside India permanently, adding a fixed RTT to every checkout coordination call and creating a data-residency question you cannot fix later without re-keying.

FOURTH — D1 IS NOT A CANDIDATE FOR THE LEDGER, at any write rate. Three independent disqualifiers: (1) hard 10 GB per database, and LetBuyy's schema is 414 tables shared across tenants — a single shared D1 is capped at 10 GB total, which a payments/orders ledger crosses quickly; (2) no interactive transactions (no BEGIN TRANSACTION), because SQLite permits one open write transaction — that directly kills the canonical-ledger pattern of SECURITY DEFINER RPCs doing SELECT ... FOR UPDATE + ON CONFLICT under one idempotency key; (3) all writes route to a single primary, and Cloudflare publishes NO writes/second figure at all. Since D1's primary is itself a Durable Object, the honest planning ceiling for D1 writes is the same ~1,000 rps single-threaded soft limit, and it is lower once you count SQL work. Read replication (still public beta as of 2025-04-10, no GA found) scales reads only, is free, one replica per region including APAC, and needs the Sessions API + bookmarks to avoid stale reads — and Sessions is binding-only, not available via REST. Verdict: Supabase Postgres stays the source of truth for money; D1's legitimate role would be per-tenant, read-heavy, non-money data (50,000 databases/account makes a database-per-merchant shard viable) with Time Travel giving free 30-day PITR. Cost note if used: rows READ are $0.001/M after 25 billion included (effectively free), rows WRITTEN are $1.00/M after 50M included — a 1,000x asymmetry that rewards read-heavy shapes and punishes write fan-out.

R2 IS THE ONE UNAMBIGUOUS WIN, and it is the cheapest lever in the stack for an India-first, image-heavy catalogue. Storage arithmetic: 100 merchants x 2 GB of product media = 200 GB => (200 - 10 free) x $0.015 = $2.85/month. At 10,000 merchants x 2 GB = 20 TB => (20,000 - 10) x $0.015 = ~$299.85/month. Operations: catalogue reads are Class B at $0.36/M with 10M/month free — 100M image origin-fetches/month => (100 - 10) x $0.36 = $32.40. Uploads are Class A at $4.50/M with 1M free — 5M product-image uploads/month => (5 - 1) x $4.50 = $18. Egress is $0, which for Indian mobile shoppers pulling 200-500 KB of imagery per product page is the single largest avoided cost versus S3. Watch two things: every multipart UploadPart is a separate Class A op (a 5 GB asset at 100 MB parts = 52 Class A ops), and Infrequent Access has a 30-day minimum duration plus 2x-2.5x operation pricing, so IA only pays off for genuinely cold archives (old invoices, shipped-order media) and will cost MORE for anything re-read. The 1-write/sec-per-object-key throttle mirrors KV's: never overwrite a fixed key like site/{id}/catalog.json under concurrency — write content-addressed keys and flip a pointer.

IMAGE TRANSFORMATION IS THE HIDDEN COST LINE. $0.50 per 1,000 unique transformations, where a unique transformation = unique (source image, parameter set) per calendar month. 100 merchants x 1,000 SKUs x 4 render sizes (thumb/grid/detail/zoom) = 400,000 unique transformations/month => (400,000 - 5,000)/1,000 x $0.50 = $197.50/month — already ~65x the R2 storage bill for the same catalogue. At 10,000 merchants the same ratio gives ~$19,997/month. The scaling levers are: cut the number of named variants (4 -> 2 saves ~50%), keep parameter strings canonical so you do not create accidental cache-key permutations (width=200 vs w=200 vs width=200,quality=85 are separate billable transformations), and let the calendar-month reset work for you on a stable catalogue rather than re-transforming on every deploy. Also note the R2 origin must be added under Images > Transformations > Sources or requests are rejected, and adding a root domain does NOT authorise its subdomains — a real footgun for {store}.letbuyy.com and per-merchant custom domains.

BUDGET SANITY CHECK AT SCALE. Durable Objects duration: 400,000 GB-s/month included, billed at 128 MB = 0.128 GB-s per wall-second, so the included allowance equals 400,000 / 0.128 = 3,125,000 object-seconds ~= 36 always-on object-days/month. One permanently resident DO consumes 2,592,000 s x 0.128 = 331,776 GB-s — inside the allowance. Two consume 663,552 GB-s => 263,552 over x $12.50/M = $3.29/month. Duration cost therefore scales with the number of SIMULTANEOUSLY RESIDENT objects, not with request count, which is why WebSocket Hibernation (zero duration while idle) and short-lived per-checkout objects matter far more than request volume ($0.15/M requests is noise). KV at 100,000 daily users x 20 page views x 5 KV reads = 10M reads/day = ~300M/month => (300 - 10) x $0.50 = $145/month — acceptable, but it makes the cacheTtl setting a direct cost lever as well as a staleness lever. Finally: every figure above is USD and pre-tax; Cloudflare has been GST-registered in India since 2023-10-01 and bills by billing address, GSTIN cannot be applied retroactively, so register the GSTIN on the account BEFORE the first invoice.
unknowns: D1 write throughput: Cloudflare publishes NO writes/second, transactions/second, or sustained-throughput figure for D1 anywhere on developers.cloudflare.com. The limits page gives only per-invocation (1,000 queries) and per-query (30 s) bounds. A D1 performance/benchmark page or a published SLO would settle it. Until then the only defensible planning number is the ~1,000 rps single-Durable-Object soft limit, since D1's primary is a Durable Object.

check.reasoning:
I independently fetched every cited Cloudflare page on 2026-08-16, and additionally pulled the raw markdown (`/index.md`) variants of the KV limits, R2 limits, how-KV-works, and KV pricing pages so that footnote text could not be lost in rendering/summarisation.

CONFIRMED VERBATIM (11 of 12):

1. KV writes to same key — https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/write-key-value-pairs/ (accessed 2026-08-16): "Workers KV has a maximum of 1 write to the same key per second. Writes made to the same key within 1 second will cause rate limiting (429) errors to be thrown." The limits table row "Writes to same key | 1 per second | 1 per second" confirms it is identical on Free and Paid. HARD.
2. KV eventual consistency — https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/concepts/how-kv-works/ : "Changes are usually immediately visible in the Cloudflare global network location at which they are made. Changes may take up to 60 seconds or more to be visible in other global network locations as their cached versions of the data time out." The page adds a detail the claim omits: "Visibility of changes takes longer in locations which have recently read a previous version of a given key (including reads that indicated the key did not exist, which are also cached locally)." — i.e. negative caching also delays propagation. Not a correction, but material for a capacity model. HARD (behavioural).
3. cacheTtl — https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/read-key-value-pairs/ : "The cacheTtl parameter must be an integer greater than or equal to 30." / "60 is the default." / "The maximum value for cacheTtl is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER." Cross-checked against the limits table row "Minimum cacheTtl | 30 seconds | 30 seconds" with footnote 2 "The maximum value is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER." DEFAULT (configurable per read), with a HARD floor of 30.
4. KV vendor guidance (what it is/isn't for) — how-kv-works confirms "read-heavy, highly cacheable workloads" (serving static assets, storing application configuration, storing user preferences, implementing allow-lists/deny-lists, caching); and the anti-patterns "support for atomic operations or where values must be read and written in a single transaction" and "If you have a write-heavy Redis-type workload where you are updating the same key tens or hundreds of times per second, KV will not be an ideal fit." Page recommends spreading writes across keys or using Durable Objects. Guidance, not a limit.
5. KV value size 25 MiB — confirmed, identical Free/Paid. HARD.
6. KV key size 512 bytes / key metadata 1024 bytes — confirmed, identical Free/Paid. HARD.
7. Keys per namespace Unlimited both plans; Storage/account 1 GB Free vs Unlimited Paid; Storage/namespace 1 GB Free vs Unlimited Paid — confirmed exactly. Note "Unlimited" on Paid is metered, not free: the pricing page bills stored data at "1 GB, + $0.50/GB-month" (USD).
8. Namespaces per account 1,000 — confirmed, identical Free/Paid.
9. Operations per Worker invocation 1000 both plans, with footnote 1 reproduced word-for-word: "Within a single invocation, a Worker can make up to 1,000 operations to external services (for example, 500 Workers KV reads and 500 R2 reads). A bulk request to Workers KV counts for 1 request to an external service." HARD.
10. list() keys per call — https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/api/list-keys/ : "The default is 1,000 keys, which is the maximum." Cursor pagination confirmed, and the warning is real: "Checking for an empty array in keys is not sufficient to determine whether there are more keys to fetch. Instead, use list_complete" (recently expired/deleted keys are iterated but not returned). HARD.
11. Reads 100,000/day Free vs Unlimited Paid; writes to different keys 1,000/day Free vs Unlimited Paid; and no documented reads-per-second or namespace-wide writes-per-second cap — confirmed; no such row exists in the limits table. Two caveats for the model, neither contradicting the claim: (a) the KV pricing page splits the Free daily allowance into separate 1,000/day buckets for keys written, keys deleted AND list requests, and states "All limits reset daily at 00:00 UTC. If you exceed any one of these limits, further operations of that type will fail with an error"; (b) Paid "Unlimited" is metered — reads "10 million/month, + $0.50/million", writes and deletes and list each "1 million/month, + $5.00/million" (USD, no egress fees). Free-tier caps are HARD; Paid is billed, effectively SOFT/metered.

CORRECTED (1 of 12 — the R2 row):
The R2 claim reproduces the headline table cells accurately, but drops the two footnotes that reduce the effective maxima. Cloudflare's own footnote 2 states the object size limit is "5 GiB less than 5 TiB, so 4.995 TiB", and footnote 4 states the max upload size is "5 MiB less than 5 GiB, so 4.995 GiB". So the real ceilings are 4.995 TiB per object and 4.995 GiB per single-part upload, not the round 5 TiB / 5 GiB. "Maximum upload parts: 10,000" and the multi-part figure 4.995 TiB are confirmed. Also confirmed and worth carrying into the model: footnote 3 — max upload size "applies to uploading a file via one request, uploading a part of a multipart upload, or copying into a part of a multipart upload. If you have a Worker, its inbound request size is constrained by Workers request limits. The max upload size limit does not apply to subrequests" — and the row "Maximum concurrent writes to the same object name (key) | 1 per second", footnote 5: "Concurrent writes to the same object name (key) at a higher rate return HTTP 429 (rate limited) responses." That R2 same-key 1/sec ceiling mirrors KV's and is a real constraint for LetBuyy asset/invoice writes. The R2 limits page publishes a single set of values with no plan differentiation, so "All plans" is fair; region is global (no ap-south-specific variation published).

No deprecated products, wrong-tier quotes, or wrong-region prices were found. The suspicious-round-number tell applies only to the R2 5 TiB / 5 GiB pair, and that is exactly where the vendor's footnotes correct it.

result.area: Vercel platform limits & pricing (Mumbai/bom1) + Next.js 16 caching semantics
result.summary: All values below were fetched from vercel.com/docs, vercel.com/legal, vercel-status.com and nextjs.org/docs on 2026-08-16; nothing is from memory. Vercel's current compute billing model is Fluid compute, metered on three axes: Active CPU (billed only while your code actually executes, paused during I/O wait), Provisioned Memory (billed for the entire instance lifetime in GB-hrs, including I/O wait), and Invocations ($0.60/1M, non-regional). Compute prices are regional; Mumbai (bom1 = ap-south-1) is $0.140/Active-CPU-hour and $0.0116/GB-hr, roughly 9% above the cheapest US regions. bom1 is a full compute region and Functions and the durable ISR cache can both be pinned there — the ISR cache region is fixed at build time from the project's default Function region, so pinning bom1 pins ISR writes/reads to bom1's higher rates ($4.40/M write units, $0.44/M read units, in 8 KB units). Function limits under Fluid: 2 GB/1 vCPU default (Pro max 4 GB/2 vCPU), 300s default duration with an 800s Pro maximum (1800s extended in beta), a hard 4.5 MB request/response payload cap (413 FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE), 250 MB uncompressed bundle, and 1,024 file descriptors shared across all concurrent executions on an instance. Concurrency auto-scales to 30,000 on Hobby and Pro (100,000 on Enterprise), but the ramp is governed by a burst limit of 1,000 concurrent executions per 10 seconds per region, scaling "may take several minutes," and exceeding it returns 503 FUNCTION_THROTTLED — there is no queue. For multi-tenancy the domain ceiling is generous but the provisioning rate is not: Pro is documented as "Unlimited" custom domains per project with an abuse soft limit of 100,000 (1,000,000 Enterprise), wildcard domains are supported on all plans provided you use Vercel's nameservers, but domain addition is rate-limited to 100 requests/hour/team. The single most dangerous multi-tenant caching fact is that Vercel's on-demand ISR revalidation "applies to the domain and deployment where you trigger it, and doesn't affect subdomains or other deployments" — so purging shopA.letbuyy.com does not purge shopA.com or any sibling tenant subdomain. Where revalidation does apply, Vercel guarantees globally consistent purging across all regions "within 300ms," and it provides genuine cache-stampede protection via automatic request collapsing (N concurrent requests to an uncached or STALE path collapse into one function invocation per region). On the framework side, the repo pins Next.js 16.1.6 while nextjs.org currently documents 16.3.1, so version drift must be verified. In Next 16 fetch is NOT cached by default; caching is opt-in. Cache Components (cacheComponents: true, introduced in 16.0.0) is the new model and is NOT enabled anywhere in this repo — which means the apps are on the "previous model" (route segment config + fetch cache), and Partial Prerendering is therefore OFF, since PPR in 16 is delivered only as the default behaviour of cacheComponents (experimental.ppr and experimental_ppr were removed). revalidateTag now requires a second cache-life profile argument (revalidateTag(tag,'max') = stale-while-revalidate); the single-arg form is deprecated, and the new Server-Action-only updateTag() gives immediate read-your-writes expiry. Tags are capped at 256 characters. Neither Next.js nor Vercel publishes a propagation latency for tag invalidation specifically — the 300ms figure is Vercel's ISR purge guarantee. Vercel's 99.99% SLA is Enterprise-only, excludes the API/CLI and Beta features, and caps credits at 50% of the monthly fee. Finally, Vercel began collecting VAT/GST from international customers for invoices issued on or after 1 April 2026, so Indian GST is additive to every USD price below.

result.capacity_implications:
WHAT BREAKS FIRST, IN ORDER.

(1) TENANT CUSTOM-DOMAIN PROVISIONING RATE — breaks at ~100 domains/hour, long before any usage limit. The ceiling is fine (Pro soft limit 100,000 domains/project) but the throughput is not: domain addition is documented at 100 requests/hour/team and verification at 50/hour/team. Onboarding 10,000 merchant apex domains = 10,000/100 = 100 hours of continuous API calls for the add alone, and 10,000/50 = 200 hours for verification — 8+ days end to end, assuming zero retries. LEVER: the *.letbuyy.com wildcard consumes exactly ONE domain slot on any plan, so subdomain tenancy is free and instant; only merchant-supplied apex domains hit this wall. Batch and backpressure the domain-attach worker, and negotiate a raise (the docs say limits are raisable) before promising same-day custom-domain onboarding at scale.

(2) MULTI-TENANT CACHE INVALIDATION CORRECTNESS — breaks immediately, at any scale. Vercel states on-demand revalidation "applies to the domain and deployment where you trigger it, and doesn't affect subdomains or other deployments." LetBuyy serves {store}.letbuyy.com AND custom domains from one project. Purging a price change on shopA.letbuyy.com does NOT purge shopA.com. With revalidate=60 on the tenant store routes and revalidate=30 on apps/storefront-runtime/src/app/store/[subdomain]/product/[productId]/page.tsx and .../collections/[slug]/page.tsx, a stale price persists on the merchant's own apex domain for up to 30-60s after an on-demand purge — and indefinitely if the purge path assumes global scope. LEVER: fan the revalidate call out across every domain a tenant owns, or accept time-based-only invalidation and shorten the interval (which trades directly against ISR write cost, item 5). Where the purge does apply, all regions converge within 300ms, so the risk is scope, not latency.

(3) FLASH-SALE CONCURRENCY RAMP — breaks at roughly 1,000 concurrent in the first 10 seconds. The 30,000 ceiling is irrelevant; the governor is 1,000 concurrent executions per 10 seconds per region, and Vercel warns scaling "may take several minutes." A single-region (bom1) deployment hitting a Diwali sale that goes 0 → 5,000 concurrent in 30 seconds has only 3 x 1,000 = 3,000 slots available, and the excess returns 503 FUNCTION_THROTTLED — rejected, not queued, not cold-started. Mitigation is structural, not configurable: maximise the fraction of requests served from CDN/ISR so they never reach a function. Request collapsing helps enormously — 1,000 simultaneous misses on the same tenant product page collapse to 1 invocation per region — but it covers ISR and Image Optimization only, NOT dynamic routes. Note that apps/storefront-runtime/src/app/page.tsx sets BOTH `export const revalidate = 300` and `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` on lines 43-44; force-dynamic wins (Next docs: it is equivalent to setting every fetch to no-store / revalidate 0), so the revalidate=300 is dead code and the platform homepage gets zero prerendering and one function invocation per request. Fix that before any launch load test.

(4) POSTGRES CONNECTIONS VIA FILE DESCRIPTORS — 1,024 file descriptors shared across ALL concurrent executions on a Fluid instance, inclusive of runtime usage. Fluid deliberately packs many concurrent requests into one instance; if each request opens a Supabase connection you exhaust descriptors well below the concurrency ceiling. LEVER: connection pooling (Supabase pooler / PgBouncer) is mandatory, not optional — and the Supabase pool ceiling will bind before Vercel's descriptor limit does.

(5) COST — arithmetic at 1,000 merchants x 1,000 pageviews/month = 1M pageviews/month, all in bom1:
  - Edge Requests: at ~25 requests/pageview (Vercel publishes no per-pageview figure — see unknowns) = 25M; 10M included, 15M billable x $2.20/M = $33.
  - Fast Data Transfer: at 1.5 MB/pageview = 1.5 TB; 1 TB included, 500 GB x $0.20 = $100.
  - Compute, checkout-shaped request (40ms active CPU, 400ms wall, 2 GB instance, in-function concurrency ~10): CPU = 1M x 0.04s = 11.1 hr x $0.140 = $1.56; Memory = 1M x 0.4s / 10 = 11.1 instance-hr x 2 GB x $0.0116 = $0.26; Invocations = 1M x $0.60 = $0.60. Total ~$2.42 per million API requests. Compute is NOT the wall — that is the central consequence of Fluid: for an I/O-bound Supabase-backed commerce API, provisioned memory (which keeps billing through I/O wait) dominates active CPU, and both are trivially small.
  - ISR WRITES ARE THE WALL. Units are 8 KB. A tenant product page's HTML+RSC payload at ~48 KB = 6 write units. Revalidation is lazy, so writes/day per page = min(requests/day, 86400/revalidate); at revalidate=30 the theoretical cap is 2,880/day/page. 1,000 tenants x 20 hot pages x even 200 actual regenerations/day x 6 units = 24M write units/day = 720M/month x $4.40/M = $3,168/month — an order of magnitude above every other line combined. CRITICAL MITIGATION, straight from the docs: "When revalidation runs and the content hasn't changed from the previous version, no ISR write units are incurred." So the real lever is determinism of rendered output, not the revalidate interval. Any new Date(), Math.random() or timestamp inside the ISR payload converts every revalidation into a billable write. Audit the tenant page render for non-determinism FIRST, then move from revalidate=30/60 to on-demand purge triggered by actual product mutations. Function invocations and Active CPU still bill on every revalidation even when no write occurs.
  - ISR reads are cheap ($0.44/M of 8 KB) and only occur on CDN miss.
  - Long tail: 1,000 tenants x 10,000 SKUs = 10M ISR entries. Storage is uncapped and free, but entries unaccessed for 31 days are evicted, so cold catalogue pages permanently pay a first-request regeneration.

(6) SINGLE-REGION AVAILABILITY — on Pro there is no function-level cross-region failover (Enterprise only). Pinning functions and the durable ISR cache to bom1 gives the best India latency and correctly co-locates with Supabase, but a bom1 outage is a total storefront outage. There is also no SLA at all on Pro: the 99.99% commitment is Enterprise-only, excludes the API and CLI, excludes Beta features, and caps credits at 50% of the monthly fee, with a 30-day written claim window. Observed CDN uptime is 99.99% over the last 90 days per vercel-status.com, but that is history, not a promise. If LetBuyy needs a contractual availability number in merchant contracts, Enterprise is the only path — and Enterprise is also what unlocks multi-tenant preview URLs, custom SSL upload, function failover, and 100,000+ concurrency.

(7) BUILD — 45 minutes per deployment is HARD on every plan including Enterprise, and this monorepo has 8 Next.js apps. Both apps/storefront-runtime/next.config.ts and apps/merchant-control-plane/next.config.ts carry custom webpack configs, and Next 16 makes Turbopack the default for `next build`, which FAILS when a webpack config is present unless you pass --webpack. Verify the CI build command explicitly. Pro allows 6,000 deployments/day and up to 500 concurrent builds, so deployment throughput is not the constraint; build wall-clock is. Also watch the 2,048 routes-per-deployment cap — Next.js auto-generates routes from dynamic segments, rewrites, redirects and headers.

(8) FRAMEWORK VERSION DRIFT — the repo pins next@16.1.6 across all 8 apps; nextjs.org currently serves 16.3.1 docs. Everything cited here attributed to v16.0.0 (cacheComponents, 'use cache', the two-argument revalidateTag, updateTag, cacheLife/cacheTag stabilisation, PPR-via-cacheComponents) is safe on 16.1.6. Features whose introducing minor is undocumented — 'use cache: remote', 'use cache: private', partialPrefetching — must be verified against node_modules/next/dist/docs/ in the installed package before being designed around. No LetBuyy app sets cacheComponents, so the entire repo is on the previous caching model: PPR is off, fetch is uncached by default, and route-segment revalidate/dynamic exports are the only caching controls in play. Adopting cacheComponents is not a rename — the docs warn it "can surface build errors for uncached data outside of <Suspense>" and requires adopting the whole model.

result.area: Supabase plans, compute/disk add-ons, Supavisor pooling, and PostgreSQL scaling behaviour (research date 2026-08-16; all facts accessed 2026-08-16)
result.summary: Supabase bills per ORGANIZATION, not per project: Free $0, Pro $25/mo, Team $599/mo, Enterprise custom. The plan fee buys almost nothing in capacity terms — the real cost and the real ceiling are the per-project Compute add-on and the disk. The compute ladder runs Nano (free only) → Micro $10 → Small $15 → Medium $60 → Large ~$111 → XL $210 → 2XL $410 → 4XL $960 → 8XL $1,870 → 12XL $2,800 → 16XL $3,730 per month, with >16XL requiring sales. The single most important non-linearity in that table: direct Postgres connections scale only 60 → 500 across the entire ladder and PLATEAU at 500 from 12XL upward, while Supavisor pooler client slots scale 200 → 12,000. Vertical scaling buys you cores, RAM and IOPS; it does not meaningfully buy you backend connections. For a Cloudflare Workers fleet this makes the transaction-mode pooler mandatory, not optional. On the critical correctness question: PgBouncer's own config documentation states that in transaction pool_mode "Server is released back to pool after transaction finishes" — the server connection is held for the whole transaction, not per statement — and PostgreSQL's SET documentation states "The effects of SET LOCAL last only till the end of the current transaction, whether committed or not." Together these establish that a per-transaction tenant GUC set via set_config(name, value, TRUE) inside an explicit BEGIN…COMMIT (or inside a single function call, which is its own implicit transaction) is SAFE under transaction-mode pooling. The corresponding hazard is precise and severe: PgBouncer documents that server_reset_query (DISCARD ALL) "is not used" in transaction pooling, so any set_config(..., FALSE) or bare SET would persist on the pooled backend and leak the tenant identity to the next client — a cross-tenant exposure, not a performance issue. PgBouncer's feature map lists SET/RESET, PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, LISTEN, session-level advisory locks and temp tables as "Never" available in transaction pooling; Supabase separately documents that Supavisor transaction mode "does not support prepared statements." Disk is the sharpest operational cliff: disk autoscales at 90% utilisation by +50%, but is limited to four modifications in a rolling 24-hour window, and when the disk fills the project "will enter read-only mode" returning `cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction` — a platform-wide write outage across every tenant simultaneously, only cleared once usage falls below 95%. IOPS is a first-class budget line, not a footnote: gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and charges $0.024 per provisioned IOPS/month, so going to the gp3 ceiling of 20,000 IOPS costs $408/mo, roughly 4x the Large compute it would sit under. Backups: Free gets none, Pro 7 days, Team 14 days, Enterprise up to 30; PITR is a paid add-on at $100/$200/$400 per month for 7/14/28-day retention, requires at least Small compute, and achieves an RPO of about two minutes. Read replicas run on the same compute size as the primary, carry 1.25x the primary's disk for WAL archives, are excluded from both the Spend Cap and Compute Credits, are asynchronously replicated, and are read-only — a same-size Large replica roughly doubles the database bill. ap-south-1 (Mumbai) exists and replicas can be placed in other regions. Egress is a unified 250 GB quota on Pro/Team at $0.09/GB over (cached $0.03/GB). There is NO published uptime SLA below Enterprise — the SLA document scopes itself to "Enterprise Customers specified in an Order Form" at 99.9% monthly with tiered service credits capped at 20% of annual fees. On the PostgreSQL side, the classic ceiling is architectural: the server "starts ('forks') a new process for each connection," each backend consumes real memory, and work_mem is per-operation so "the total memory used could be many times the value of work_mem." RLS policy expressions are "evaluated for each row prior to any conditions or functions coming from the user's query" except for leakproof functions — which is exactly why Supabase's own guidance to index policy columns and wrap function calls in (select …) to force a cached initPlan reports improvements of 99.9%+. FOR UPDATE waits for the concurrent transaction to end and holds the lock until transaction end, so hot-row contention serializes independently of compute size. Autovacuum's default scale factor of 0.2 means a high-churn orders table waits for 20% of its rows to become dead before being vacuumed. PostgreSQL's official partitioning rule of thumb is that "the size of the table should exceed the physical memory of the database server."

facts.metric: Is SET LOCAL / set_config(name, value, TRUE) inside an explicit transaction SAFE under transaction-mode pooling? (LetBuyy per-transaction tenant GUC)
facts.value: YES — SAFE. PgBouncer pool_mode=transaction: "Server is released back to pool after transaction finishes" (NOT after each statement). PostgreSQL SET docs: SET LOCAL "takes effect for only the current transaction. After COMMIT or ROLLBACK, the session-level setting takes effect again" and "The effects of SET LOCAL last only till the end of the current transaction, whether committed or not." The whole transaction therefore executes on one pinned backend and the GUC is discarded at COMMIT/ROLLBACK. set_config "provides equivalent functionality" to SET.

facts.subject: PgBouncer / Supavisor transaction pooling
facts.metric: Session-state leakage risk when is_local=FALSE (cross-tenant correctness hazard)
facts.value: UNSAFE. server_reset_query default is "DISCARD ALL" but: "When transaction pooling is used, the server_reset_query is not used, because in that mode, clients must not use any session-based features." A session-scoped set_config(name, value, FALSE) or bare SET therefore PERSISTS on the pooled backend and is inherited by the next client assigned that connection — leaking one tenant's site_id GUC to another tenant's query.
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. server_reset_query_always (default 0) exists specifically to patch "broken setups that run applications that use session features over a transaction-pooled PgBouncer".

facts.subject: PgBouncer SQL feature map for pooling modes
facts.metric: Features NOT available in transaction pooling

LOAD statement: Yes / NEVER. Session-level advisory locks: Yes / NEVER. WITHOUT HOLD cursor: Yes / Yes. facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17
facts.metric: Process model — why connection count is the classic ceiling
facts.value: "The PostgreSQL server can handle multiple concurrent connections from clients. To achieve this it starts ('forks') a new process for each connection." "From that point on, the client and the new server process communicate without intervention by the original postgres process." "Thus, the supervisor server process is always running, waiting for client connections, whereas client and associated server processes come and go."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. One OS process per connection is the architectural root cause of the connection ceiling — it is not a tunable.

The default is typically 100 connections, but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb). This parameter can only be set at server start." Increasing its value leads to higher allocation of those resources, including shared memory." superuser_reserved_connections default: "three connections". reserved_connections default: "zero connections".

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17
facts.metric: Memory sizing — work_mem multiplication across connections
facts.value: work_mem default: "four megabytes (4MB)". Official caution: "a complex query might perform several sort and hash operations at the same time, with each operation generally being allowed to use as much memory as this value specifies before it starts to write data into temporary files. Also, several running sessions could be doing such operations concurrently. Therefore, the total memory used could be many times the value of work_mem; it is necessary to keep this fact in mind when choosing the value." shared_buffers default "typically 128 megabytes (128MB)"; guidance: "a reasonable starting value for shared_buffers is 25% of the memory in your system" and "it is unlikely that an allocation of more than 40% of RAM to shared_buffers will work better than a smaller amount." maintenance_work_mem default: "64 megabytes (64MB)".
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. This is the arithmetic behind the connection ceiling: N connections × concurrent sort/hash ops × work_mem must fit in the ~60-75% of RAM not held by shared_buffers.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17 Row-Level Security
facts.metric: When policy predicates are evaluated relative to user query quals
facts.value: "This expression will be evaluated for each row prior to any conditions or functions coming from the user's query. (The only exceptions to this rule are leakproof functions, which are guaranteed to not leak information; the optimizer may choose to apply such functions ahead of the row-security check.)" "Superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass the row security system... Table owners normally bypass row security as well, though a table owner can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY." "Referential integrity checks, such as unique or primary key constraints and foreign key references, always bypass row security."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. 'Evaluated for each row' is the whole performance story: a non-leakproof function in a policy runs per row before your WHERE clause can filter anything.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17 Row-Level Security
facts.metric: Documented cost of referencing other tables inside policies
facts.value: "If it is necessary to consult other rows or other tables to make a policy decision, that can be accomplished using sub-SELECTs, or functions that contain SELECTs, in the policy expressions. Be aware however that such accesses can create race conditions that could allow information leakage if care is not taken." And: "heavy concurrent use of row share locks on the referenced table could pose a performance problem, especially if updates of it are frequent."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. Directly relevant: an RLS policy that joins to `sites` to verify ownership takes row share locks on `sites` on every query, on a table that is updated by merchant settings changes.

facts.subject: Supabase RLS performance guidance
facts.metric: Documented optimisations and published improvement figures
facts.value: (1) Index policy columns — "Make sure you've added indexes on any columns used within the Policies" — benchmark showed 99.94% improvement adding a user_id index. (2) Wrap functions in select — use `(select auth.uid())` instead of `auth.uid()`; this creates an initPlan that "cache[s] the results per-statement, rather than calling the function on each row" — improvements 94.97% to 99.993%. (3) Specify roles with TO — "prevent the policy...from running for any anon users" — 99.78% improvement in one benchmark. (4) Minimize joins — reorganize to "select the filter criteria into a set" and use IN/ANY — up to 99.78%. (5) Add explicit filters in client queries rather than relying on the policy as an implicit WHERE — 94.74%.
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. Caveat from the docs: you can only wrap a function in (select …) if its result does not depend on row data. The `0003 auth rls initplan` lint in Supabase's Performance Advisor flags unwrapped calls.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17
facts.metric: FOR UPDATE blocking and queueing semantics
facts.value: "FOR UPDATE causes the rows retrieved by the SELECT statement to be locked as though for update. This prevents them from being locked, modified or deleted by other transactions until the current transaction ends. That is, other transactions that attempt UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, SELECT FOR NO KEY UPDATE, SELECT FOR SHARE or SELECT FOR KEY SHARE of these rows will be blocked until the current transaction ends; conversely, SELECT FOR UPDATE will wait for a concurrent transaction that has run any of those commands on the same row, and will then lock and return the updated row (or no row, if the row was deleted)."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. The waiter blocks for the FULL remaining duration of the holder's transaction — so any slow work (an HTTP call, a large insert) inside a transaction holding a FOR UPDATE lock directly multiplies contention.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17
facts.metric: Row lock duration, reader impact, and write amplification
facts.value: "Row-level locks do not affect data querying; they block only writers and lockers to the same row." "Row-level locks are released at transaction end or during savepoint rollback, just like table-level locks." "PostgreSQL doesn't remember any information about modified rows in memory, so there is no limit on the number of rows locked at one time. However, locking a row might cause a disk write, e.g., SELECT FOR UPDATE modifies selected rows to mark them locked, and so will result in disk writes." FOR NO KEY UPDATE is a weaker lock "also acquired by any UPDATE that does not acquire a FOR UPDATE lock"; FOR KEY SHARE "blocks other transactions from performing DELETE or any UPDATE that changes the key values".
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. SELECT FOR UPDATE is a WRITE — it consumes IOPS. A high-volume lock-then-check pattern burns provisioned IOPS even when nothing is ultimately updated. Prefer FOR NO KEY UPDATE where FK key columns are untouched, to avoid blocking FK checks.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17 autovacuum

"The launcher will distribute the work across time, attempting to start one worker within each database every autovacuum_naptime seconds."

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17 vacuuming
facts.metric: What prevents dead-row reclamation and causes unbounded bloat
facts.value: "the row version must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions." Three documented blockers: (1) "End long-running open transactions. You can find these by checking pg_stat_activity for rows where age(backend_xid) or age(backend_xmin) is large." (2) "Resolve old prepared transactions... checking pg_prepared_xacts for rows where age(transactionid) is large." (3) "Drop any old replication slots. Use pg_replication_slots to find slots where age(xmin) or catalog_xmin is large." Guidance: "administrators should strive to use standard VACUUM and avoid VACUUM FULL"; wraparound requires vacuuming "every table in every database at least once every two billion transactions."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. Read replicas create replication slots — an unhealthy or lagging replica holds back xmin on the PRIMARY and causes primary-side bloat. This couples replica health to primary disk growth.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17 partitioning
facts.metric: Official rule of thumb for WHEN partitioning is worthwhile
facts.value: "These benefits will normally be worthwhile only when a table would otherwise be very large. The exact point at which a table will benefit from partitioning depends on the application, although a rule of thumb is that the size of the table should exceed the physical memory of the database server." Documented benefits: query performance when "most of the heavily accessed rows... are in a single partition or a small number of partitions" because "Partitioning effectively substitutes for the upper tree levels of indexes, making it more likely that the heavily-used parts of the indexes fit in memory"; and "Bulk loads and deletes can be accomplished by adding or removing partitions" — DROP TABLE / DETACH PARTITION "entirely avoid the VACUUM overhead caused by a bulk DELETE."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. Concrete threshold for LetBuyy: on Large (8 GB RAM) an orders table crosses this line around 8 GB; on 4XL (64 GB) around 64 GB.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17 partitioning
facts.value: "The query planner is generally able to handle partition hierarchies with up to a few thousand partitions fairly well, provided that typical queries allow the query planner to prune all but a small number of partitions. Planning times become longer and memory consumption becomes higher when more partitions remain after the planner performs partition pruning." "Another reason to be concerned about having a large number of partitions is that the server's memory consumption may grow significantly over time, especially if many sessions touch large numbers of partitions. That's because each partition requires its metadata to be loaded into the local memory of each session that touches it." "Never just assume that more partitions are better than fewer partitions, nor vice-versa."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. This is decisive against partition-per-tenant: 10,000 merchants = 10,000 partitions, above the "few thousand" guidance, and each session touching many tenants loads per-partition metadata into backend-local memory.

facts.subject: PostgreSQL 17
facts.metric: SET LOCAL interaction with savepoints and SET-option functions
facts.value: "The effects of SET or SET LOCAL are also canceled by rolling back to a savepoint that is earlier than the command." "A special case is SET followed by SET LOCAL within a single transaction: the SET LOCAL value will be seen until the end of the transaction, but afterwards (if the transaction is committed) the SET value will take effect." "If SET LOCAL is used within a function that has a SET option for the same variable (see CREATE FUNCTION), the effects of the SET LOCAL command disappear at function exit." "Issuing this outside of a transaction block emits a warning and otherwise has no effect."
facts.note: Accessed 2026-08-16. Two operational traps for a tenant GUC: (a) ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT silently clears the tenant GUC — subsequent statements in the same transaction run with no tenant context; (b) a SECURITY DEFINER function declared with its own SET clause discards the caller's SET LOCAL on exit.

facts.subject: PostgREST (Supabase REST layer)
facts.metric: How per-request transaction settings are applied
facts.value: PostgREST wraps each request: "START TRANSACTION; -- <Access Mode> <Isolation Level> -- <Transaction-scoped settings> -- <Main Query> END;".
